say: This tool asks two separate questions about a password. Is it hard to guess, and has it already been stolen. Those are not the same question, and a password can pass one and fail the other badly.
Turning on show, so you can read what I type.
Here is a password that looks like a reasonable corporate one. Capital letter, digits, a symbol, eleven characters. It would pass most password policies you have ever been forced to obey.

The meter scores it fair. That score comes from zxcvbn, which does not count character classes. It looks for dictionary words, names, dates, keyboard walks and repeats, and prices the password at what a real attacker's guess list would cost. Summer is a word and twenty twenty four is a date, so the symbol at the end buys almost nothing.
All of that happened in your browser. Nothing was sent anywhere. The second question cannot be answered locally, though, because it needs a database of stolen passwords.

So it uses k anonymity. Your password is hashed here, and only the first five characters of that hash are sent to Have I Been Pwned. They send back every leaked hash starting with those five, and the match is found on your machine. They never learn which one you asked about.
Found in over three thousand breached passwords. The meter said fair. The breach database says attackers already have this one on a list. That gap is the entire reason both checks exist.
Three unrelated words and a number, joined by hyphens. No capital letter and no digit-for-letter substitution, so it would still fail some corporate policies outright.

Very strong, and the estimated offline crack time is far beyond anything worth attempting. Length and unpredictability are what actually matter. The symbol rules everyone types out of habit mostly produce passwords that are hard for people to remember and easy for machines to guess.
